title: Verifier–Agent Co-Design Reduces Verifier-Induced Blocking in Agentic NetOps Planning
abstract: We test whether integrating runtime verifier feedback into an LLM planner (co‑design) reduces verifier-induced blocking of safe plans relative to a static post‑hoc verifier for synthetic NetOps change tasks. Following a preregistered paired design (CNSM2026-AgenticNetOps-GuardedGVR-v1), we executed 200 intent→configuration tasks in a deterministic containerized emulator using a hosted gpt-5-mini adapter. Primary analysis used complete paired runs (N=187). Guarded planning (runtime verifier feedback) achieved 187/187 safe completions (1.000) versus 179/187 (0.9572) for baseline; paired absolute difference = 0.0427807487, exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.0078125, paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.01604278075, 0.07486631016] (bootstrap resamples=10000, seed=1729). These confirmatory results support the preregistered primary hypothesis (H1). The preregistered secondary non‑inferiority hypothesis on planning latency (H2) is unconfirmed: the registered analysis executor did not produce the paired latency diagnostics required for the pre‑registered non‑inferiority test, so H2 remains inconclusive. We report deterministic execution artifacts, the shared‑initial generation semantics used in the paired design, a reproducibility mapping to archived artifacts, and a focused threats‑to‑validity discussion bounding generalization to other models and production networks.

sections.introduction: Large language models and agentic LLM architectures are being adopted for NetOps tasks (intent→configuration translation, change planning, limited self‑healing). Recent surveys emphasise that operational reliability depends strongly on orchestration, verifier design, and runtime tooling rather than model token‑accuracy alone [https://openalex.org/W7161354925, https://openalex.org/W7114889968]. A common operational tension is the "verifier tax": aggressive verifiers block unsafe plans but can also prevent otherwise valid safe plans when agents do not adapt planning to verifier constraints [https://openalex.org/W7203715746]. We evaluate whether a verifier–agent co‑design—where the planner receives deterministic runtime verifier feedback and may adapt candidate plans—reduces verifier‑induced blocking without materially degrading planning latency. Contributions: (1) a preregistered paired experiment comparing static post‑hoc verification (baseline) to guarded planning with runtime verifier feedback (co‑design) on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks; (2) confirmatory evidence that co‑design materially reduced verifier‑induced blocking in this emulated corpus (absolute +0.04278, p=0.0078125); (3) explicit reporting of unexecuted preregistered analyses (including an unconfirmed latency non‑inferiority hypothesis), a concise reproducibility mapping to archived artifacts, and a discussion of validity threats and operational implications.
sections.related_work: Surveys and systematic reviews document rapid growth of LLM‑based NetOps/AIOps work and call for workflow‑centred evaluation that includes verifiers, orchestration, and rollback semantics [https://openalex.org/W7161354925, https://openalex.org/W4411700982]. Generate–validate–repair and retrieval‑augmented pipelines mitigate hallucination and structural failures but do not eliminate them; runtime monitoring reduces unsafe actions in controlled settings while a specification/translation bottleneck limits task‑level formal guarantees [https://openalex.org/W7114889968, https://openalex.org/W7203715746]. Failure taxonomies highlight hallucinations, DSL/structured‑output errors, and incorrect topology/state assumptions as recurring NetOps failure modes [https://openalex.org/W4412158322]. These findings motivated a focused empirical test of verifier–agent co‑design to address the verifier‑tax tension (design gap G1 in our preregistration).
sections.methodology: Preregistration and overall design: The study was preregistered as CNSM2026-AgenticNetOps-GuardedGVR-v1 prior to observing final outcomes. The design is a paired confirmatory study over 200 deterministic synthetic tasks (three task classes: routing, ACL, VLAN; two topology classes). Each task instance was executed twice (baseline vs guarded) and pairing preserved; primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test: exact McNemar two‑sided with paired bootstrap 95% CI (resamples=10000, seed=1729). Key pre‑registered execution contracts (adapter family, model, validator, retry/exclusion rules) were followed and are recorded in the execution manifest. Generation semantics (shared initial candidate): The preregistration fixed generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" and independent_condition_generation = false. Concretely, for each task a single initial candidate configuration was generated (shared_initial_generation stage) and recorded; both baseline and guarded condition runs began from that shared initial candidate. Under guarded planning, the planner could observe deterministic runtime verifier feedback and—per the preregistered generate–validate–repair policy—invoke up to one repair attempt (repair stage) to adapt the plan before final scoring. This semantics reduces uncontrolled variance between paired runs (the same initial candidate is compared under different verifier integration strategies) and isolates the effect of runtime verifier feedback and repair. It also implies that discordant outcomes reflect guarded runs adapting the shared candidate (repair invoked) or the verifier path differing post‑generation; observed stage counts indicate shared_initial_generation=200 and repair=8 (see reproducibility mapping below). Inclusion/exclusion and missingness: The preregistered retry policy allowed up to two deterministic infra retries; incomplete pairs (one condition failing after retries) were excluded from the primary analysis (complete_pair_primary). Sensitivity analyses (planned) included treating incomplete pairs as failures; the sensitivity run treating incomplete pairs as failures was not produced by the registered analysis executor and therefore is reported here as unexecuted (see Results). Validator and scoring: A deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) applied syntactic and intent/workflow policy checks; a run is scored as a safe end‑to‑end completion only if validator.final_state.valid is true and required workflow policies are satisfied. Analysis executor: Confirmatory analysis used registered executor 'paired_binary_analysis_v1' which produced the primary paired contingency counts, exact McNemar p‑value, and bootstrap CI. Preplanned secondary estimand H2 (latency non‑inferiority, 20% margin) required paired latency diagnostics from the executor; those diagnostics were not produced in the executor's secondary_results output and thus H2 is unconfirmed (see Results).
sections.results: Execution accounting and primary dataset: planned_episode_count=400 (200 pairs × 2); completed_episode_count=374; failed_episode_count=26; model_calls_used=208. After deterministic exclusions per preregistration, the primary confirmatory dataset comprised 187 complete pairs. Primary outcome (confirmatory): baseline_success_count = 179/187 = 0.9572192513368984; guarded_success_count = 187/187 = 1.000. Paired contingency: n_11=179, n_10=8 (guarded success, baseline failure), n_01=0, n_00=0. Paired absolute difference = 0.04278074866310155. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.0078125. Paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.016042780748663103, 0.0748663101604278] (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000). These confirmatory numbers are produced by the registered analysis executor and support H1. Unexecuted or unconfirmed preregistered analyses: (1) The preregistered sensitivity analysis that treats incomplete pairs as failures (planned secondary confirmatory check) was not produced by the registered analysis executor outputs and therefore is unexecuted for this report. (2) The preregistered latency non‑inferiority test (H2) is unconfirmed: latency diagnostics required for the paired non‑inferiority calculation were not produced by the registered analysis executor's secondary_results; accordingly H2 is reported as inconclusive rather than supported. Exploratory diagnostics: provider audit shows stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=200 and repair=8; the eight discordant pairs (n_10=8) align with repair invocations or planner adjustments under guarded planning that avoided baseline failures. Missingness: 13 pairs were both missing (both_missing_pairs=13) due to deterministic infra/adapter failures and were excluded per preregistration (complete_pair_primary). Reproducibility mapping (principal reported numbers → archived artifacts): complete_pair_count=187 and condition summary (baseline successes 179, guarded 187) are in analysis/condition_summary.csv (sha256 prefix ef339baf); paired contingency counts (n_11=179, n_10=8, n_01=0, n_00=0) are in analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (sha256 prefix d6a5b155); exact McNemar p and bootstrap CI originate from the registered analysis outputs and are recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl (sha256 prefix 130f65d3); raw episode records and per‑task validator traces are in execution/raw_results.jsonl (sha256 prefix 6a95bf3e); the run used model_configuration.json (sha256 prefix 916b386b) declaring the adapter/model. The full initial master prompt archive is provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba) and preregistration manifest (preregistration_sha256 prefix 668ae85f). All referenced artifacts appear in the supplied execution and analysis manifests described in the evidence bundle.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: In this deterministic synthetic/emulated corpus, co‑design (runtime verifier feedback with allowed repair) increased the safe end‑to‑end completion probability by ≈4.28 percentage points (absolute) relative to static post‑hoc verification; the bootstrap CI and exact McNemar p‑value from the preregistered executor support H1 under the preregistered analysis plan. The observed discordant pattern (n_10=8, n_01=0) and the repair stage count (repair=8) indicate that guarded planning enabled corrective adaptations to an initial shared candidate that baseline post‑hoc verification would have blocked. Role of shared_initial_candidate: The predeclared shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation=false) reduces generation variance between paired runs and isolates the effect of verifier integration and repair. It can bias the paired comparison toward conservative estimates of co‑design benefit if sharing produces similar downstream candidates that both conditions would accept, and it can concentrate differences where repair is invoked. This semantics was preregistered and is reflected in the execution manifest (shared_initial_generation=200). Threats to validity: internal validity benefits from deterministic pairing, fixed seeds, and preregistered exclusions, but prompt sensitivity and single‑model dependence remain. Construct validity is limited by the deterministic validator approximating operational correctness via DSL and workflow checks; it cannot fully emulate human operator judgment, rollback semantics, or multi‑vendor device idiosyncrasies. External validity: experiments used a single declared adapter (gpt‑5‑mini), a deterministic synthetic task generator, and containerized emulator topologies; results do not imply production readiness or cross‑model generality. Unexecuted preregistered checks: sensitivity analyses treating incomplete pairs as failures and the latency non‑inferiority confirmatory test were not produced by the registered analysis executor outputs; omission weakens the breadth of confirmatory claims and is explicitly reported here as an unresolved preregistered check. Operational implications and next steps: co‑design patterns that surface verifier constraints to planners and permit bounded repair can reduce verifier‑induced blocking; next steps are systematic multi‑model, multi‑testbed replication and human‑in‑the‑loop evaluations to measure latency/throughput trade‑offs and production risk.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment comparing static post‑hoc verification and runtime verifier feedback (co‑design) for LLM‑driven NetOps planning in a deterministic emulated corpus. Guarded planning produced a statistically significant increase in safe completion rate on 187 complete pairs (absolute +0.0427807487, exact McNemar p=0.0078125, paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.01604278075, 0.07486631016]). The result supports the preregistered primary hypothesis (H1) in this constrained setting. The preregistered latency non‑inferiority hypothesis (H2) is unconfirmed because the registered analysis executor did not produce the paired latency diagnostics required for that test; accordingly H2 remains inconclusive. Limitations (single model, synthetic/emulated tasks, unexecuted preregistered secondary checks) restrict generalization. We provide deterministic execution and analysis artifacts, a reproducibility mapping to principal numbers, and recommend replication across models, richer emulators, and human‑in‑the‑loop designs to evaluate production relevance and latency trade‑offs.

disclosure_statement: Mandatory Disclosure Statement (CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track). LLM(s) and model identifiers: experiments used a hosted adapter declared as gpt-5-mini via the 'hosted_netops_gvr_v1' adapter family (see execution/model_configuration.json; model config sha256 prefix 916b386b). Exact initial master‑prompt reference: provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Human role and autonomy boundary: the Research Director selected the broad topic family (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the autonomy lock; after the autonomy lock the AI system autonomously performed literature review, study selection, preregistration, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, peer‑review‑style internal checks, and manuscript drafting. Pre‑lock development: infrastructure and rehearsal work occurred before the autonomy lock and are explicitly not used as empirical evidence. Preregistration: study preregistered as CNSM2026-AgenticNetOps-GuardedGVR-v1 (preregistration manifest sha256 prefix 668ae85f). Orchestration and tools permitted: run used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter, a deterministic synthetic intent→configuration task generator, deterministic containerized emulator images (two topology classes), and deterministic validator 'deterministic_netops_validator_v5'; repair‑stage calls were permitted per the preregistered generate–validate–repair policy. Model‑call budget and execution: maximum_model_calls set to 400; actual model_calls_used=208; execution followed the frozen retry and exclusion policy; deterministic retry policy allowed up to two infra retries; incomplete pairs were excluded per preregistration. Artifact provenance and reproducibility: raw outputs, execution manifests, model configuration, task manifests, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are recorded in the supplied execution and analysis manifests (representative artifact prefixes cited in the manuscript). Post‑lock human editing: no manual human editing, rewriting, or selective improvement of technical content was performed after the autonomy lock; all manuscript text and analyses are derived from archived autonomous‑run artifacts. Deviations and restarts: execution manifest records completed_episode_count=374, failed_episode_count=26; all retries and infra failures were handled per the preregistered retry policy and logged. Limitations of autonomy: internet and hosted‑model access were available to the autonomous pipeline as declared; no private proprietary datasets or restricted human adjudications were used. This disclosure identifies the initial master prompt archive and its SHA‑256 as required.
limitations: Single‑model limitation: experiments used one declared adapter (gpt‑5‑mini); results may not generalize across other LLMs or fine‑tuned variants.

Synthetic‑emulation scope: tasks derive from a deterministic synthetic intent→configuration generator and containerized emulator topologies; the deterministic validator approximates operational correctness but does not replicate full production rollback, monitoring, or human‑operator decision processes.
External validity: production networks, multi‑vendor device semantics, and human operator procedures are not represented; results do not establish production safety or readiness.

Latency hypothesis unconfirmed: preregistered non‑inferiority H2 on planning latency was not confirmed because the registered analysis executor did not produce required paired latency diagnostics; H2 remains inconclusive.

Possible residual pretraining exposure: deterministic contamination checks excluded known pre‑lock artifacts but cannot eliminate uncertainty about broader model pretraining exposure to conceptually similar public artifacts.

Missingness: 13 pairs were both missing (both conditions failed after retries) and were excluded from the primary analysis per preregistration; planned sensitivity analyses treating incomplete pairs as failures were not produced by the registered executor and remain unexecuted.
